Appendix A Algorithmic details on NQS optimization for ground-state search

A.1 Natural gradients and advanced optimizers

In Section II.1, we introduced the real and imaginary-time TDVP and defined the Fisher information matrix. A noteworthy observation is that imaginary-time TDVP is formally equivalent to the optimization of the cost function in Eq. (8) via natural gradient descent, a seminal algorithm known as Stochastic Reconfiguration (SR) [112], recently improved by min-SR [30]. This equivalence follows from the definition of natural gradient, obtained by applying the inverse Fisher information matrix to the standard gradient:

𝐠𝜽=S−1​(𝜽)​∇𝜽.\mathbf{g}_{\bm{\theta}}=S^{-1}(\bm{\theta})\bm{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}\,. (41)

Indeed, a first-order numerical integration of the imaginary-time TDVP equations leads to an iterative parameter update

𝜽⁡(τ+δ​τ)=𝜽⁡(τ)−δ​τ​S−1​(𝜽⁡(τ))​F​(𝜽⁡(τ)),\bm{\theta}(\tau+\delta\tau)=\bm{\theta}(\tau)-\delta\tau S^{-1}\big(\bm{\theta}(\tau)\big)F\big(\bm{\theta}(\tau)\big)\,, (42)

which corresponds to a Natural Gradient Descent step with step size δ​τ\delta\tau since

𝐠𝜽​E​(𝜽)=S−1​(𝜽)​∇𝜽E​(𝜽)=S−1​(𝜽)​F​(𝜽).\mathbf{g}_{\bm{\theta}}E(\bm{\theta})=S^{-1}(\bm{\theta})\bm{\nabla}_{\bm{\theta}}E(\bm{\theta})=S^{-1}(\bm{\theta})F(\bm{\theta})\,. (43)

As briefly mentioned in Section II.1, natural gradients can be combined with advanced stochastic optimizers developed for deep learning. While this strategy has not been explored in the NQS literature to our knowledge, it has been studied in the broader machine learning community. For example, works such as [66, 79] precondition the stochastic gradient with an (approximate) inverse Fisher information matrix and apply momentum before updating parameters. Ref. [73] further proposes a unified framework for accelerated natural gradient descent.

In practice, an optimizer maintains an auxiliary state α\alpha, and given the (natural) gradient, returns both the parameter update and the new auxiliary state. As stated in Section IV, in this work, we combine SR with momentum, where the auxiliary state is a velocity vector storing an exponentially decaying average of past natural gradients.

Algorithm 1 presents a high-level overview of NQS optimization for ground-state search, potentially combining natural gradients with an advanced optimizer. As remarked in Section II.1, we collectively refer to all these variants as SR in the remainder of the text.

A.2 Variational Quantum Annealing pseudo-code

As explained in Section II.3, an alternative approach to ground-state optimization with NQS relies on interpolating from an easy to a hard regime by tuning a parameter in the Hamiltonian. The resulting high-level implementation of VQA for optimizing a variational ansatz (typically an NQS) is illustrated in Algorithm 2. We note that, in Ref. [55], the parametric Hamiltonian is defined slightly differently compared to Eq. (10), precisely as H⁡(s)=HT+(1−s)​H0H(s)=H_{\mathrm{T}}+(1-s)H_{0}, with H0=−Bx∑iσixH_{0}=-B^{x}\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{x} and Bx≫1B^{x}\gg 1. Although Ref. [55] uses Adam and simple gradients to train RNN wavefunctions, it is possible to extend this approach to other NQS architectures and to natural gradients.

Appendix B Standard analytical results on Boltzmann Machines

In Section II.4, we introduced the RBM as the simplest efficiently trainable version of generic BMs. Starting from Eq. (16), the joint probability function over visible and hidden variables reads

p⁡(𝐯,𝐡,𝜽)=Z−1​exp⁡{𝐯T​W​𝐡+𝐛T​𝐯+𝐜T​𝐡},p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})=Z^{-1}\exp\{\mathbf{v}^{T}W\mathbf{h}+\mathbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{h}\}\,, (44)

where

Z=∑𝐯′,𝐡′exp⁡(−E⁡(𝐯′,𝐡′,𝜽)).Z=\sum_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\exp{-E(\vb v',\vb h';\boldsymbol{\theta})}\,. (45)

This partition function ZZ has been proven to be intractable [75], implying that the explicit computation of a normalized marginal probability distribution for the visible units is also intractable. Nonetheless, it is possible to exactly trace out the hidden variables to obtain the unnormalized marginal distribution

pRBM​(𝐯,𝜽)=∑𝐡p⁡(𝐯,𝐡,𝜽)\displaystyle p_{\text{\tiny RBM}}(\mathbf{v};\bm{\theta})=\sum_{\mathbf{h}}p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta}) (46)
=Z−1​exp⁡(𝐛T​𝐯)​∏j=0Nhcosh⁡{cj+∑i=0Nvvi​Wi​j}.\displaystyle=Z^{-1}\exp{\vb b^T \vb v}\prod_{j=0}^{N_{h}}\cosh\left\{c_{j}+\sum_{i=0}^{N_{v}}v_{i}W_{ij}\right\}\,.

The inability to compute the exact partition function does not constitute a serious limitation, as multiple methods have been devised to approximate it [48], and its explicit computation is often unnecessary in practice. For instance, Monte Carlo methods circumvent the problem of computing the partition function by computing unweighted averages over the samples drawn from the model.

The key property of RBMs that enables efficient sampling and training stems from the bipartite structure of their interaction graph. Indeed, conditioned on the hidden units, the visible units are mutually independent, and vice versa. This fact allows us to explicitly compute the normalized conditional probabilities

The normalized conditional probabilities read:

p⁡(vi|𝐡;𝜽)\displaystyle p(v_{i}|\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta}) =p~​(vi|𝐡;𝜽)p~​(vi=+1|𝐡;𝜽)+p~​(vi=−1|𝐡;𝜽)\displaystyle=\frac{\tilde{p}(v_{i}|\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})}{\tilde{p}(v_{i}=+1|\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})+\tilde{p}(v_{i}=-1|\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})} (48)
=exp⁡{(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)​vi}exp⁡{(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)}+exp⁡{−(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)}\displaystyle=\frac{\exp\left\{\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)v_{i}\right\}}{\exp\left\{\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)\right\}+\exp\left\{-\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)\right\}}
=exp⁡{(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)​(vi−1)}​σ​[2​(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)],\displaystyle=\exp\left\{\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)(v_{i}-1)\right\}\sigma\left[2\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)\right]\,,

where σ⁡(x)\sigma(x) denotes the logistic sigmoid function. The normalized probability for the ii-th visible unit to have value +1+1, conditioned on all hidden variables, simplifies to

p⁡(vi=+1|𝐡;𝜽)=σ⁡[2​(bi+∑j=1NhWi​j​hj)],p(v_{i}=+1|\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})=\sigma\left[2\left(b_{i}+\sum_{j=1}^{N_{h}}W_{ij}h_{j}\right)\right]\,, (49)

and a similar expression holds for the value −1-1. Since the difference between visible and hidden units is only formal, the conditional probability for the hidden units given the visible ones can be computed in the same way:

p⁡(hj=+1|𝐯;𝜽)=σ⁡[2​(cj+∑i=1NvWi​j​vi)].p(h_{j}=+1|\mathbf{v};\bm{\theta})=\sigma\left[2\left(c_{j}+\sum_{i=1}^{N_{v}}W_{ij}v_{i}\right)\right]\,. (50)

The mutual independence of visible units conditioned on hidden units, and vice versa, enables efficient block Gibbs sampling of the joint probability function p⁡(𝐯,𝐡,𝜽)p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta}). By starting from a random configuration, a Markov chain can be constructed with the update rule that, at each iteration, all visible units are simultaneously sampled conditioned on the hidden units, and then all hidden units are sampled conditioned on the visible units. Moreover, these samples can be drawn via exact sampling of the conditional probability in Eqs. (49) and (50). Such an alternating conditional sampling efficiently generates samples from the joint probability distribution p⁡(𝐯,𝐡;𝜽CLOSEp(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta}) [29, 48], which are necessary both during training and inference.

During training, the RBM parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are typically optimized by minimizing the negative log-likelihood using variants of gradient descent. The gradient of such objective function can be expressed in terms of expectation values and two-point correlations between hidden and visible units [11], which are efficiently estimated via Gibbs sampling. At the inference stage, the trained model would be used to compute the expectation values of functions of the visible units f⁡(𝐯)f(\bf v) over the marginal probability distribution pRBM​(𝐯,𝜽)p_{\text{\tiny RBM}}(\mathbf{v};\bm{\theta}) in Eq. (46), which cannot be explicitly normalized. This expectation value, denoted as ⟨⋯⟩RBM\langle\cdots\rangle_{\text{\tiny RBM}}, is equal to the expectation value of the same function over the joint probability p⁡(𝐯,𝐡;𝜽CLOSEp(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta}):

⟨f⁡(𝐯)⟩RBM=∑𝐯p⁡(𝐯)​f​(𝐯)∑𝐯p⁡(𝐯)\displaystyle\expectationvalue{f(\vb v)}_{\text{\tiny RBM}}=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v})f(\mathbf{v})}{\sum_{\mathbf{v}}p(\mathbf{v})} (51)
=∑𝐯,𝐡p⁡(𝐯,𝐡)​f​(𝐯)∑𝐯,𝐡p⁡(𝐯,𝐡)=⟨f⁡(𝐯)⟩p⁡(𝐯,𝐡).\displaystyle=\frac{\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h})f(\mathbf{v})}{\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h})}=\expectationvalue{f(\vb v)}_{p(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h})}\,.

This allows us to efficiently estimate it by performing block Gibbs sampling and using the normalized conditional probability functions in Eqs. (49) and (50).

The more general case of DBMs in Eq. (17) is similarly treated. The joint probability function is given by

p⁡(𝐱,𝜽)=1Z​e∑l=0NL−1𝐱(l)​T​W(l)​𝐱(l+1)+∑l=0NL𝐛(l)​T​𝐱(l).p(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})=\frac{1}{Z}e^{\sum_{l=0}^{N_{L}-1}\mathbf{x}^{(l)T}W^{(l)}\mathbf{x}^{(l+1)}+\sum_{l=0}^{N_{L}}\mathbf{b}^{(l)T}\mathbf{x}^{(l)}}\,. (52)

where

Z=∑𝐱′exp⁡(−E⁡(𝐱′,𝜽)).Z=\sum_{\mathbf{x}^{\prime}}\exp{-E(\vb x'; \boldsymbol{\theta})}\,. (53)

The computation of the marginal probability function for the visible units, as done for the RBM in Eq. (46), is now intractable even in its unnormalized version. Nonetheless, similarly to the case of RBMs, the variables can be rearranged into a bipartite graph, with odd layers on one side and even layers on the other. This immediately implies that when we condition on the units in the even layers, the variables in the odd layers become independent, and vice versa. More precisely, it is enough to condition on the adjacent layers, and the explicit computation of the normalized conditional probability leads to

\displaystyle p⁡(xi(l)=+1|𝐱(l−1),𝐱(l+1);𝜽)=\displaystyle p(x^{(l)}_{i}=+1|\mathbf{x}^{(l-1)},\mathbf{x}^{(l+1)};\bm{\theta})= (54)
σ⁡[(∑jWj​i(l−1)​xj(l−1)+∑jWi​j(l)​xj(l+1)+bi(l))],\displaystyle\sigma\!\left[2\!\left(\!\sum_{j}W^{(l-1)}_{ji}x^{(l-1)}_{j}\!+\!\sum_{j}W^{(l)}_{ij}x^{(l+1)}_{j}\!+\!b^{(l)}_{i}\!\right)\!\right]\!\,,

with slightly different expressions for the first and last layers. Analogously to the RBM case, this conditional independence enables efficient block Gibbs sampling by updating all units in only two iterations. Firstly, one can update all the units in the even layers (including the l=0l=0 visible layer) as a block, conditioned on the units in the odd layers, and, secondly, all the hidden units in the odd layers conditioned on the units in the even ones. The samples can be drawn via exact sampling of the conditional probability in Eq. (54).

Appendix C Previous quantum extensions of Boltzmann Machines

Several extensions of BMs and specifically RBMs to quantum spin systems have been previously proposed. For quantum systems, the fundamental object is not the probability function, but rather the wavefunction, which is a complex-valued function representing the probability amplitudes.

C.1 pmRBM and cRBM

A conceptually straightforward extension proposed in Ref. [118] and known as pmRBM uses two independent RBMs to model the phase and the modulus of the wavefunction. The wavefunction is expressed in the spin eigenbasis, which is commonly associated with the eigenstates of the Pauli-Z operators:

ψ⁡(𝐱,𝜽)=pRBMm​(𝐱,𝜽m)​exp⁡{i​pRBMp​(𝐱,𝜽p)},\psi(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})=\sqrt{p_{\text{\tiny RBM}}^{\mathrm{m}}(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{m}})}\exp\{i\,p_{\text{\tiny RBM}}^{\mathrm{p}}(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}_{\mathrm{p}})\}\,, (55)

where pRBM​(𝐱,𝜽)p_{\text{\tiny RBM}}(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta}) denotes the RBM unnormalized marginal probability distribution (see Appendix B). Here, 𝜽=(𝜽m,𝜽p)\bm{\theta}=(\bm{\theta}_{m},\bm{\theta}_{p}) are real parameters, and 𝐱\mathbf{x} is a collective label for a spin eigenstate in the Pauli-Z eigenbasis. Current literature suggests that the artificial separation of modulus and phase information is suboptimal, making the learning problem more challenging, regardless of the specific ANN model used. Almost all recent NQS applications [106] utilize ANNs parameterized by complex variational parameters to output a complex number representing the wavefunction amplitude. This approach was proposed in the context of RBMs in Ref. [25], which is based on the idea of promoting the probability distribution defined by an RBM to quantum amplitudes by introducing complex parameters. The resulting ansatz, commonly referred to as cRBM, reads

ψ⁡(𝐱,𝜽)=e∑i=0Nvbi​xi​∏j=0Nhcosh⁡({cj+∑i=0Nvxi​Wi​j}),\psi(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})=e^{\sum_{i=0}^{N_{v}}b_{i}x_{i}}\prod_{j=0}^{N_{h}}\cosh{\left\{ c_j + \sum_{i=0}^{N_v} x_i W_{ij}\right\}}\,, (56)

which is formally equivalent to the unnormalized marginal probability distribution of an RBM (see Appendix B), with the only difference that 𝜽=(W,𝐛,𝐜)\bm{\theta}=(W,\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c}) are now complex parameters.

In combination with the standard SR algorithm, this ansatz has been successfully used to find a variety of quantum ground-states with remarkable precision [25, 130, 122, 87] and in the context of NQA in Ref. [120]. However, the possibility of efficient block Gibbs sampling is lost in the cRBM, so one must utilize Metropolis-Hastingss sampling with local update rules, which has significantly longer autocorrelation times, making it slower and more computationally expensive.

C.2 DBM wavefunctions

A possible quantum extension of DBMs based on the same principle of the cRBM was introduced in Ref. [24] and reads

ψ⁡(𝐱,𝜽)=∑𝐱(l)l>0e∑l=0NL−1𝐱(l)​T​W(l)​𝐱(l+1)+∑l=0NL𝐛(l)​T​𝐱(l).\psi(\mathbf{x};\bm{\theta})\!=\!\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathbf{x}^{(l)}\\ l>0\end{subarray}}e^{\sum_{l=0}^{N_{L}-1}\mathbf{x}^{(l)T}W^{(l)}\mathbf{x}^{(l+1)}+\sum_{l=0}^{N_{L}}\mathbf{b}^{(l)T}\mathbf{x}^{(l)}}. (57)

The original reference also provides an interesting constructive approach that does not require a variational optimization of the DBM parameters. However, due to the intractability of the summation in Eq. (57) and the restrictive conditions under which efficient block Gibbs sampling of the model is possible, this variational ansatz has only been applied to small-scale benchmarks.

C.3 Quantum Boltzmann Machines

Another possible extension, dubbed Quantum Boltzmann Machine (QBM), was proposed in Ref. [11]. The units of the BM are promoted to quantum spins, and the state of the system is described as the exponential of a transverse-field Ising Hamiltonian

HQBM=−∑aΓaσax−∑abaσaz−∑a​bwa​bσzaσzbH_{\text{QBM}}=-\sum_{a}\Gamma_{a}{\sigma}_{a}^{x}-\sum_{a}b_{a}{\sigma}_{a}^{z}-\sum_{ab}w_{ab}{\sigma}^{z}_{a}{\sigma}^{z}_{b} (58)

yielding the density matrix operator

ρ=1Z​exp⁡{−HQBM}.\rho=\frac{1}{Z}\exp\{-H_{\text{QBM}}\}\,. (59)

The presence of non-commuting terms poses significant challenges in training the model, as detailed in the original reference [11], which applies this framework to address classical machine learning tasks. Later, Ref. [92] used a simplified version of QBMs without hidden units to learn the ground-states of quantum systems through a hybrid quantum-classical method inspired by the variational quantum eigensolver.

Appendix D Analytical results for Boltzmann Quantum States

In this Section, we report additional results on BQS and their relationship to the cRBM introduced in [24] and described in Appendix C. We adopt the same notation as in Section III.

D.1 Ground-state structure of the extended Hilbert space and expectation values

The BQS formalism describes both visible and hidden spins as quantum spins in an extended Hilbert space ℋv​h=ℋv⊗ℋh\mathcal{H}_{vh}=\mathcal{H}_{v}\otimes\mathcal{H}_{h}. Although the two Hamiltonians HvH_{v} and Hv​h=Hv⊗𝕀hH_{vh}=H_{v}\otimes\mathbb{I}_{h} share the same spectrum, the ground-state of the extended system can have a non-trivial entanglement structure. Specifically, if HvH_{v} has a degenerate ground-state, then there exist ground-states of Hv​hH_{vh} that are entangled across the visible/hidden partition, rather than simple tensor products of two pure states. Let HvH_{v} be a Hamiltonian with a dd-fold degenerate ground-state, let {|Ψva⟩}a=1d\{\ket{\Psi_{v}^{a}}\}_{a=1}^{d} be a set of orthonormal ground states, and let {|Φvb⟩}b=1dimℋv−d\{\ket{\Phi_{v}^{b}}\}_{b=1}^{\dim\mathcal{H}_{v}-d} be a set of orthonormal higher energy eigenstates so that {|Ψva⟩,|Φvb⟩}\{\ket{\Psi_{v}^{a}},\ket{\Phi_{v}^{b}}\} forms a complete orthonormal basis of ℋv\mathcal{H}_{v}. Then, any state |ψv​h⟩\ket{\psi_{vh}} of the extended system can be expanded as

|ψv​h​(G,E)⟩=\displaystyle\ket{\psi_{vh}(G,E)}= ∑a,𝐡Ga​𝐡​|Ψva⟩⊗|𝐡⟩\displaystyle\sum_{a,\mathbf{h}}G_{a\mathbf{h}}\ket{\Psi_{v}^{a}}\otimes\ket{\mathbf{h}} (60)
+\displaystyle+ ∑b,𝐡Eb​𝐡​|Φvb⟩⊗|𝐡⟩,\displaystyle\sum_{b,\mathbf{h}}E_{b\mathbf{h}}\ket{\Phi_{v}^{b}}\otimes\ket{\mathbf{h}}\,,

and its energy expectation value is

⟨ψv​h​(G,E)​|Hv​h|​ψv​h​(G,E)⟩⟨ψv​h​(G,E)|ψv​h​(G,E)⟩=∑a,𝐡|Ga​𝐡|2​⟨Ψva​|Hv|​Ψva⟩+∑b,𝐡|Eb​𝐡|2​⟨Φvb​|Hv|​Φvb⟩∑a,𝐡|Ga​𝐡|2+∑b,𝐡|Eb​𝐡|2.\frac{\expectationvalue{\psi_{vh}(G,E)|H_{vh}|\psi_{vh}(G,E)}}{\expectationvalue{\psi_{vh}(G,E)|\psi_{vh}(G,E)}}=\frac{\sum_{a,\mathbf{h}}|G_{a\mathbf{h}}|^{2}\expectationvalue{\Psi_v^a|H_v|\Psi_v^a}+\sum_{b,\mathbf{h}}|E_{b\mathbf{h}}|^{2}\expectationvalue{\Phi_v^b|H_v|\Phi_v^b}}{\sum_{a,\mathbf{h}}|G_{a\mathbf{h}}|^{2}+\sum_{b,\mathbf{h}}|E_{b\mathbf{h}}|^{2}}\,. (61)

Hence, by the variational principle, the ground states of Hv​hH_{vh} take the form

|Ψv​h​(G)⟩=∑a,𝐡Ga​𝐡​|Ψva⟩⊗|𝐡⟩,\ket{\Psi_{vh}(G)}=\sum_{a,\mathbf{h}}G_{a\mathbf{h}}\ket{\Psi_{v}^{a}}\otimes\ket{\mathbf{h}}\,, (62)

and variational energy minimization in the extended Hilbert space can generally yield entangled states that do not decompose into the tensor product of a state of the visible spins and a state of the hidden spins, provided the variational ansatz can describe entanglement between the two partitions.

Indeed, if we denote by Ψ⁡(𝐯,𝐡,𝜽)=⟨𝐯,𝐡|Ψ⁡(𝜽)⟩\Psi(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})=\expectationvalue{\vb v, \vb h|\Psi(\boldsymbol{\theta})} the (converged) BQS ansatz written in the computational basis {|𝐱⟩}={|𝐯,𝐡⟩}\{\ket{\mathbf{x}}\}=\{\ket{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}\}, we can formally trace out the hidden degrees of freedom. This generally yields a mixed state for the visible spins:

ρv=∑𝐯,𝐯′,𝐡Ψ⁡(𝐯,𝐡,𝜽)​Ψ⁡(𝐯′,𝐡,𝜽)¯​|𝐯⟩​⟨𝐯′|.\rho_{v}=\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h}}\Psi(\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})\overline{\Psi(\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h};\bm{\theta})}\ket{\mathbf{v}}\bra{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}\,. (63)

The summation over 𝐡\mathbf{h} required to compute the matrix elements is tractable only in the case of the RBQS ansatz, as an analytical expression can be obtained for the reduced density operator

ρvRBQS\displaystyle\rho_{v}^{\text{RBQS}} =∑𝐯,𝐯′exp⁡([∑ibi​vi−b¯i​vi′])​∏jcosh⁡{∑i(Wi​j​vi−W¯i​j​vi′)+cj−c¯j}​|𝐯⟩​⟨𝐯′|.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}\exp{\left[\sum_i b_i v_i - \overline{b}_i v'_i\right]}\prod_{j}\cosh\left\{\sum_{i}(W_{ij}v_{i}-\overline{W}_{ij}v_{i}^{\prime})+c_{j}-\overline{c}_{j}\right\}\ket{\mathbf{v}}\bra{\mathbf{v}^{\prime}}\,. (64)

On the contrary, and similarly to the classical case, this summation cannot be performed analytically for the general DBQS ansatz. Nonetheless, in practical applications, we typically need to compute the ground-state expectation value of operators OvO_{v} acting solely on visible spins. D.2 Relation to the cRBM architecture and universality of DBQS

Here, we show that applying a projection operator to the hidden partition collapses the visible spins into a pure state. Then, we demonstrate that specific projections reduce the RBQS and DBQS ansatzes to the cRBM and DBM wavefunctions of Refs. [25, 24], establishing that the DBQS framework generalizes these earlier models.

Given a pure state of the hidden spins |χh⟩\ket{\chi_{h}}, applying the projection operator Pχ=𝕀v⊗|χh⟩​⟨χh|P_{\chi}=\mathbb{I}_{v}\otimes\ket{\chi_{h}}\bra{\chi_{h}} to a generic state of the extended system |ψv​h⟩\ket{\psi_{vh}} yields

(𝕀v⊗|χh⟩​⟨χh|)​|ψv​h⟩\displaystyle(\mathbb{I}_{v}\otimes\ket{\chi_{h}}\bra{\chi_{h}})\ket{\psi_{vh}} (68)
=∑𝐯,𝐡|𝐯,𝐡⟩​⟨𝐯,𝐡|​(𝕀v⊗|χh⟩​⟨χh|)​∑𝐯′,𝐡′|𝐯′,𝐡′⟩​⟨𝐯′,𝐡′|ψv​h⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}\ket{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}\bra{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}(\mathbb{I}_{v}\otimes\ket{\chi_{h}}\bra{\chi_{h}})\sum_{\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\ket{\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\expectationvalue{\vb v',\vb h'|\psi_{vh}}
=∑𝐯,𝐡,𝐯′,𝐡′|𝐯,𝐡⟩​⟨𝐯|𝐯′⟩​⟨𝐡|χh⟩​⟨χh|𝐡′⟩​⟨𝐯′,𝐡′|ψv​h⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h},\mathbf{v}^{\prime},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\ket{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}\expectationvalue{\vb v|\vb v'}\expectationvalue{\vb h|\chi_h}\expectationvalue{\chi_h|\vb h'}\expectationvalue{\vb v',\vb h'|\psi_{vh}}
=∑𝐯,𝐡,𝐡′|𝐯,𝐡⟩​⟨𝐡|χh⟩​⟨χh|𝐡′⟩​⟨𝐯,𝐡′|ψv​h⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h},\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\ket{\mathbf{v},\mathbf{h}}\expectationvalue{\vb h|\chi_h}\expectationvalue{\chi_h|\vb h'}\expectationvalue{\vb v,\vb h'|\psi_{vh}}
=∑𝐯[∑𝐡′⟨χh|𝐡′⟩​⟨𝐯,𝐡′|ψv​h⟩]​|𝐯⟩⊗∑𝐡⟨𝐡|χh⟩​|𝐡⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\left[\sum_{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\expectationvalue{\chi_h|\vb h'}\expectationvalue{\vb v,\vb h'|\psi_{vh}}\right]\ket{\mathbf{v}}\otimes\sum_{\mathbf{h}}\expectationvalue{\vb h|\chi_h}\ket{\mathbf{h}}
=∑𝐯[∑𝐡′⟨χh|𝐡′⟩​⟨𝐯,𝐡′|ψv​h⟩]​|𝐯⟩⊗|χh⟩.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\left[\sum_{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\expectationvalue{\chi_h|\vb h'}\expectationvalue{\vb v,\vb h'|\psi_{vh}}\right]\ket{\mathbf{v}}\otimes\ket{\chi_{h}}\,.

Now consider the special case where |ψv​h⟩=|ΨR​B​Q​S⟩\ket{\psi_{vh}}=\ket{\Psi_{RBQS}} is an (unnormalized) RBQS wavefunction as in Eq. (20), and

|χh⟩=|→h⟩=∑𝐡|𝐡⟩\ket{\chi_{h}}=\ket{\rightarrow_{h}}=\sum_{\mathbf{h}}\ket{\mathbf{h}}

is the (unnormalized) uniform superposition over all hidden configurations. Then, the projected state becomes

(𝕀v⊗|→h⟩​⟨→h|)​|ΨR​B​Q​S⟩\displaystyle(\mathbb{I}_{v}\otimes\ket{\rightarrow_{h}}\bra{\rightarrow_{h}})\ket{\Psi_{RBQS}} (69)
=∑𝐯[∑𝐡′exp⁡{𝐯T​W​𝐡′+𝐛T​𝐯+𝐜T​𝐡′}]​|𝐯⟩⊗|→h⟩\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\left[\sum_{\mathbf{h}^{\prime}}\exp\left\{\mathbf{v}^{T}W\mathbf{h}^{\prime}+\mathbf{b}^{T}\mathbf{v}+\mathbf{c}^{T}\mathbf{h}^{\prime}\right\}\right]\ket{\mathbf{v}}\otimes\ket{\rightarrow_{h}}
=∑𝐯[e∑i=0Nvbi​vi​∏j=0Nhcosh⁡{cj+∑i=0Nvvi​Wi​j}]​|𝐯⟩⊗|→h⟩.\displaystyle=\!\sum_{\mathbf{v}}\!\left[\!e^{\sum_{i=0}^{N_{v}}b_{i}v_{i}}\prod_{j=0}^{N_{h}}\cosh\!{\left\{\!c_{j}\!+\!\sum_{i=0}^{N_{v}}v_{i}W_{ij}\!\right\}}\right]\!\ket{\mathbf{v}}\!\otimes\!\ket{\rightarrow_{h}}\!\,.

Hence, the state in which the visible spins are found exactly matches the cRBM wavefunction introduced in Ref. [25]. Similarly, projecting a DBQS wavefunction with two hidden layers onto the state |→h⟩\ket{\rightarrow_{h}} for the hidden units yields the DBM wavefunction of Ref. [24]. This establishes that both the cRBM and DBM can be viewed as specific subclasses of the RBQS and DBQS ansatzes, respectively. Remarkably, since the DBM wavefunction family has been proven to be a universal approximator of quantum states [42], the DBQS inherits this expressive power, while potentially representing complex quantum states more effectively.

D.3 Dataset–free initialization of the DBQS parameters

Typical uses of DBMs in machine learning rely on greedy layer‑wise pretraining [48]. In the NQA setting such pretraining yields no benefit: the first few optimization steps rapidly overwrite any pre‑trained weights, effectively undoing the layer‑wise initialization long before the algorithm approaches the hard part of the evolution. To our knowledge, however, dataset‑free initialization of DBMs has not been systematically explored. Motivated by Ref. [126], which shows that Xavier initialization [44] improves training of canonical RBMs, we adopt a Xavier‑normal initialization scheme for the variational parameters: all biases are set to zero, and the real and imaginary parts of the weights connecting layer (l)(l) and layer (l+1)(l+1) are sampled independently from a normal distribution with 00 mean and variance a/(N(l)+N(l+1))a/(N_{(l)}+N_{(l+1)}), where N(l)N_{(l)} is the number of units in layer ll and aa is a gain factor (here fixed at a=10−2a=10^{-2}).

If the initial DBQS parameters are drawn from 𝒩⁡(0,σ2)\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma^{2}), the ensemble‑averaged log‑amplitude 𝔼⁡[log⁡ψ⁡(𝐱)]\mathbb{E}[\log\psi(\mathbf{x})] is exactly zero for any spin configuration |𝐱⟩\ket{\mathbf{x}}, and the variance scales linearly with σ\sigma. Hence, for sufficiently small gain factor, the untrained network already provides a reasonable representation of the uniform superposition state for all spins (visible and hidden). This is chosen as the initialization of the variational DBQS wavefunction.

D.4 Comparison of block Gibbs chains and Metropolis-Hastings chains

In Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) sampling, successive samples are typically correlated because each new sample is generated from the previous one, rather than drawn independently from the target distribution. This autocorrelation reduces the efficiency of the sampling procedure by decreasing the number of effectively independent samples obtained from the chain. The degree of this dependence can be quantified using the integrated autocorrelation time (IAT), which provides a measure of the number of iterations required, on average, to produce an effectively independent sample.

Let {𝐱t}t=0N−1\{\mathbf{x}_{t}\}_{t=0}^{N-1} denote a stationary Markov chain, and consider a real-valued function of the chain state f⁡(𝐱)f(\mathbf{x}). The autocorrelation function at lag tt is defined as

ρf​(t)=𝔼⁡[(f⁡(𝐱0)−μf)​(f⁡(𝐱t)−μf)]σf2\rho_{f}(t)=\frac{\mathbb{E}[(f(\mathbf{x}_{0})-\mu_{f})(f(\mathbf{x}_{t})-\mu_{f})]}{\sigma_{f}^{2}} (70)

where μf\mu_{f} and σf2\sigma_{f}^{2} denote the mean and variance of f⁡(x)f(x) on the chain. The IAT can be estimated by

τf=1+2​∑t=1+∞ρf​(t)\tau_{f}=1+2\sum_{t=1}^{+\infty}\rho_{f}(t) (71)

In practice, the infinite sum is truncated at a lag where ρf​(t)\rho_{f}(t) becomes negligible. When considering multiple functions, one should consider the highest IAT across all functions to ensure reliable statistical estimates. In the context of spin systems, the functions of interest are typically the individual spins: fi​(𝐱)=xif_{i}(\mathbf{x})=x_{i}.

For MCMC algorithms employing local update rules, such as the single-spin flip Metropolis-Hastings (MH) chain, the autocorrelation time often scales at least linearly with the system size. Specifically, if only a fraction α\alpha of the NsN_{s} spins is updated in each iteration, then roughly 1/α1/\alpha iterations are required for every spin to have an opportunity to be updated once, corresponding to one sweep over the system. This local nature of the dynamics can lead to large autocorrelation times. In Metropolis-Hastings algorithms, rejected proposals further increase correlations because the chain remains in the same state after a rejection, whereas Gibbs updates are always accepted by construction.

To draw a quantitative comparison, we run both Gibbs and MH chains across several DBQS realizations as the system size increases. We measure the IAT for the magnetization along zz (on the computational basis) for each spin, and take the maximum value. Figure 8 shows the maximum IAT for untrained DBQS with 33 hidden layers and a hidden unit density per layer of 11. For each system size, we average over 1010 realizations of the dataset-free initialization described in the previous section. As expected, we find that block Gibbs chains systematically converge faster and have autocorrelation times of order O⁡(1)O(1), whereas single-spin flip MH chains show IAT values of O⁡(N)O(N). Similar results are observed empirically during training of the variational DBQS wavefunction.

Appendix E Algorithmic details on Neural Quantum Annealing

This section provides supplementary technical details on NQA. In particular, we specify the exact implementation of our code and list all tunable hyperparameters, commenting on their effect on algorithmic behavior and computational cost. From a broad algorithmic perspective, NQA is an advanced Monte Carlo method: its runtime scales polynomially, and it does not guarantee finding the exact solution in a strict mathematical sense. Despite the lack of performance guarantees, for many spin glass problems described in Section V, it successfully finds the best or best-known solution, or a good approximation. As for any Monte Carlo algorithm, the quality of this approximation can be systematically improved through careful hyperparameter tuning.

E.1 Algorithmic overview

As discussed in Section IV, NQA combines standard SR with momentum acceleration and persistent Gibbs chains enabled by our novel DBQS architecture. The update step is shown in Algorithm 3, and recursively executed throughout the optimization. It comprises three actions:

  1. 1.

    Sampler update: Advance the persistent chains with a few block-Gibbs updates and draw a set of configurations;

  2. 2.

    Natural-gradient evaluation: Compute the natural gradient;

  3. 3.

    Parameter update: Update the variational parameters and the optimizer state.

This update step is embedded into the full NQA optimization showcased in Algorithm 4, which comprises the following actions:

  1. 1.

    Initialization: The parameters of the DBQS are drawn from the Xavier-normal distribution as described in Section D.3. An ensemble of block-Gibbs chains is then initialized and thermalized.

  2. 2.

    Pre-training: The ansatz is first trained to approximate the ground state of the initial Hamiltonian at s0=0s_{0}=0. When the initial Hamiltonian is chosen as H0=−∑iσixH_{0}=-\sum_{i}\sigma_{i}^{x}, this step can be skipped because, as argued in Section D.3, the Xavier initialization already yields an accurate approximation of its ground state.

  3. 3.

    Iterative annealing: For each intermediate annealing point sjs_{j}, we perform a few NQA update steps. In practice, a single step for each value of sjs_{j} (j=1,…,NA−1j=1,\dots,N_{A}-1) is usually sufficient to keep the state close to the variational adiabatic path and successfully approximate the final target state.

  4. 4.

    Fine-tuning: Finally, additional update steps are carried out at sNA=1s_{N_{A}}=1 in order to suppress any residual excited-state components of the wavefunction.

E.2 NQA Hyperparameters

In the following, we enumerate the tunable hyperparameters of NQA, organizing them into five groups based on their role in the algorithm.

E.2.1 Annealing Hyperparameters

These parameters characterize the annealing schedule and the parametric Hamiltonian H⁡(s)H(s) in Eq. (32).

  • •

    Number of annealing steps NAN_{A}: it fixes the number of discretized values of the annealing parameter along the schedule, precisely given by 0=s0<s1<⋯<sNA=10=s_{0}<s_{1}<\cdots<s_{\tiny{N_{A}}}=1.

  • •

    Number of warm-up update steps NWN_{W}: number of NQA_UpdateSteps to perform for s0=0s_{0}=0 to prepare the initial ground-state.

  • •

    Number of updates steps per annealing step NUN_{U}: number of NQA_UpdateSteps performed for each intermediate value of sjs_{j}, for j=1,…,NA−1j=1,\dots,N_{A}-1. Using a number of updates per step equal to one is sufficient for most classical and quantum applications, by selecting a sufficiently large number of annealing steps NAN_{A}, as anticipated in Section IV.

  • •

    Number of fine-tuning update steps NFN_{F}: number of NQA_UpdateSteps performed at sNA=1s_{N_{A}}=1. Although this final refinement does not seem to yield any performance improvement on classical problems, it empirically improves the performance for quantum ground states.

  • •

    Annealing field scale A>0A>0: multiplicative prefactor of the initial Hammiltonian H0H_{0}. Typically, during the annealing dynamics, the system undergoes a phase transition (a crossover, for finite systems) from a paramagnetic to a spin glass phase (additional phase transitions, such as perturbative crossings, may also occur). Heuristically, NQA is expected to work better when such a transition occurs somewhat close to s≈1/2s\approx 1/2. Indeed, if the transition happens for s≈0s\approx 0, there is almost no difference between NQA and standard NQS optimization on the target problem Hamiltonian, since the hard regime is immediately reached. On the contrary, when the transition happens for s≈1s\approx 1, the variational ansatz may not have enough time to relax on the target ground-state in the hard regime, and computational resources may be wasted in the easy regime. Correctly tuning AA such that the transition occurs neither too soon nor too late during the annealing can be achieved automatically through hyperparameter optimization.

  • •

    Catalyst field scale BB: multiplicative prefactor of HCH_{C}, included for the same reason as the annealing field scale. If we explicitly fix B=0B=0, no catalyst is utilized.

E.2.2 Optimizer Hyperparameters

As stated in the main text, we use natural gradients with momentum. Hence, the optimizer hyperparameters are the learning rate η>0\eta>0, momentum 0≤μ<10\leq\mu<1, and diagonal shift λd\lambda_{d}. The diagonal shift does not appear to be critical for the algorithm’s performance. On the contrary, selecting optimal learning rate and momentum values is crucial and should be done automatically via hyperparameter optimization, as the optimal values strongly depend on the target problem and on the NQS architecture.

E.2.3 DBQS Hyperparameters

  • •

    Number of hidden layers NLN_{L}: number of hidden layers in the DBQS architecture defined in Section III.

  • •

    Hidden-units density per layer α\alpha: ratio between the number of hidden spins in each hidden layer (assumed to be layer-independent) and the number of visible (physical) spins in the visible layer.

  • •

    Parameters type (real or complex): whether to use real or complex variational parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta}. Real parameters can be used for stoquastic Hamiltonians as the instantaneous ground state can be represented by real positive amplitudes. Using real parameters enforces this inductive bias, reduces the ansatz’s capacity, and may yield lower computational cost and runtime.

E.2.4 Block Gibbs sampler Hyperparameters

  • •

    Number of samples NsamplesN_{\text{samples}}: number of samples to generate to compute observables, such as the local energy.

  • •

    Number of chains NchainsN_{\text{chains}}: number of persistent block Gibbs chains to run in parallel. We recommend having one chain per sample, if possible, as this yields a faster runtime and guarantees that the samples are uncorrelated.

  • •

    Number of thermalization steps NthermN_{\text{therm}}: number of Gibbs chain steps to thermalize the chains at the beginning of the algorithm. (Recommended values may be 100−1000100-1000).

  • •

    Number of sweep updates NsweepsN_{\text{sweeps}}: number of block Gibbs updates to perform in between drawing successive samples from a given chain. (Recommended 10−10010-100).

E.3 Computational complexity

The computational complexity of NQA is linear in the number of calls of the NQA_UpdateStep function, which amounts to NW+NF+NA​NUN_{W}+N_{F}+N_{A}N_{U}. The first two terms in the sum are usually negligible, as is the computational cost of the rest of the code; hence, the overall computational cost is essentially proportional to NA​NUN_{A}N_{U} times the computational cost of a NQA_UpdateStep function call. The latter comprises three contributions; we will now analyze them one by one.

First, propagating each persistent block Gibbs chain for NsweepsN_{\text{sweeps}} sweeps through a DBQS with NLN_{L} hidden layers requires O⁡(Nsweeps​NL)O(N_{\text{sweeps}}N_{L}) matrix multiplications of matrices of size O⁡(Nv)O(N_{v}) times a vector of size O⁡(Nv)O(N_{v}). This operation has computational complexity of O⁡(Nv2)O(N_{v}^{2}), for a total complexity of O⁡(Nsweeps​NL​Nv2)O(N_{\text{sweeps}}N_{L}N_{v}^{2}), and updating all the chains costs O⁡(Nsamples​Nsweeps​NL​Nv2)O(N_{\text{samples}}N_{\text{sweeps}}N_{L}N_{v}^{2}).

Secondly, the complexity of computing the natural gradients via SR scales as O⁡(Nparams3)O(N_{\text{params}}^{3}) or via min–SR O⁡(Nparams​Nsamples2+Nsamples3)O(N_{\textrm{params}}N_{\textrm{samples}}^{2}+N_{\textrm{samples}}^{3}) [30] for the matrix pseudoinverse. Since a DBQS has number of parameters O⁡(Nspins2​Nlayers)O(N_{\text{spins}}^{2}N_{\text{layers}}), the SR route costs O⁡(Nspins6​Nlayers3)O(N_{\text{spins}}^{6}N_{\text{layers}}^{3}), and min–SR reduces this to O⁡(Nspins2​Nlayers​Nsamples2+Nsamples3)O(N_{\text{spins}}^{2}N_{\text{layers}}N_{\text{samples}}^{2}+N_{\text{samples}}^{3}). There is also the calculation of the logarithmic derivatives, which is just the computation of averages over the previously generated samples, at a cost of O⁡(Nparams​Nsamples)O(N_{\textrm{params}}N_{\textrm{samples}}). Concerning the local energies, as mentioned in the main text, they involve a matrix multiplication of O⁡(Nv2)O(N_{v}^{2}), and a scalar product O⁡(Nv)O(N_{v}). Total cost via min–SR is O⁡(Nparams​Nsamples2+Nsamples3)O(N_{\textrm{params}}N_{\textrm{samples}}^{2}+N_{\textrm{samples}}^{3})

Thirdly, evaluating the local energy and related observables is O⁡(Nspins2)O(N_{\text{spins}}^{2}), while the subsequent momentum–SGD update of the parameters is negligible.

Collecting all terms, the per-step complexity for the practical (min–SR) implementation is

O⁡(Nspins2​Nlayers​(Nsamples2+Nsweeps)+Nsamples3),O(N_{\text{spins}}^{2}N_{\text{layers}}(N_{\text{samples}}^{2}+N_{\text{sweeps}})+N_{\text{samples}}^{3}), (72)

which remains tractable for the modest Nsamples,Nsweeps≪Nspins2N_{\text{samples}},N_{\text{sweeps}}\ll N_{\text{spins}}^{2} typically required in practice.

With carefully chosen settings, NQA can provide exact solutions for instances of spin glasses with hundreds of spins on a consumer laptop with a single NVIDIA RTX3060m GPU.

Appendix F Additional information on the hyperparameter optimization (HPO)

Identifying optimal hyperparameters for NQA is challenging, as the hyperparameters detailed in Appendix E are non-trivially correlated in their effect on algorithmic performance. The optimal choice depends on the problem at hand, and as for most machine learning algorithms, there is no universal set of hyperparameters that works every time for every problem. To find the optimal hyperparameters for a given problem, we use Optuna [7], a framework for black box optimization commonly used in the machine learning community for hyperparameter tuning. The specific algorithms we use are the Tree-structured Parzen Estimator (TPE) [18] and the Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (CMA-ES) [50], depending on the computational budget and the parallelization capabilities available.

We recommend setting a fixed budget for the total number of trials and sampling the first ∼80%\sim 80\% with CMA-ES and the remaining ∼20%\sim 20\% with TPE. This will generate sufficient statistics to support claims of optimality with actual data. Moreover, we recommend setting a wall-clock time limit per trial to prevent the HPO from selecting hyperparameter configurations that lead to ever-increasing computational complexity.

F.1 HPO for SK benchmarks

The HPO for the SK benchmark instances with cRBM and RBQS ansatzes are performed by only optimizing the learning rate and momentum, as shown in Table 1, whereas all other hyperparameters are fixed as reported in Table 2. Here, no maximum time limit per run is set, as each run requires the same runtime within this simplified HPO. The HPO for the DBQS ansatz is reported in Table 3, with fixed settings in Table 4. Here, we implement a 2-hour wall-clock time limit per trial to avoid computationally inefficient hyperparameter combinations; successful runs usually take ≤30\leq 30 minutes of wall-clock time on our hardware. In both cases, new trial settings are sampled via TPE. Note that the RBQS can function with a significantly smaller number of sweep updates than the cRBM; the large number reported in Table 2 was chosen to give the cRBM and RBQS ansatz the same HPO setting to obtain a fair comparison.

F.2 HPO for JSSP benchmarks

The ranges and settings for the HPO studies on the JSSP benchmark instances are reported in Table 5 and Table 6. New trial settings are sampled via CMA-ES; here, we implement a 4-hour wall-clock time limit per trial to prune computationally inefficient hyperparameter combinations. Successful runs take 5−505-50 minutes of wall-clock time on our hardware.

F.3 HPO for transverse-field SK benchmarks

The ranges and settings for the HPO studies on the transverse-field SK benchmark instances with N=16N=16 are reported in Table 7 and Table 8, and those for the N=100N=100 benchmarks are reported in Table 9 and Table 10. The first 100 trials are sampled via CMA-ES, and the last 50 via TPE. Here, we implement a 1-hour wall-clock time limit per trial to prune computationally inefficient hyperparameter combinations.

Appendix G Additional data on the SK benchmark

Table 11 reports the typical energy errors on the N=200N=200 benchmarks for all the combinations explored. Figure 9 and Figure 10 show the energy error histograms for the set-ups not shown in the main text.

Appendix H Additional information on the transverse-field SK benchmark

H.1 Additional results on the benchmark

The energies obtained for the N=16N=16 benchmark are reported in Table 12. Table 13 shows the results for our benchmark instances with N=100N=100 spins. Additional figures showing the data for all the examined instances are available at [72] or [1] in the Paper/Figures/FiguresExtra.
